name: Theyyam
tagline: North Malabar’s living ritual — colour, music and possession
summary: Theyyam is a living ritual-dance tradition of North Malabar (especially Kannur), where performers become possessed deities in colourful makeup, music and fire rites. A powerful, community-rooted…
description: Theyyam is a living ritual-art of North Malabar performed in kavus (sacred groves), ancestral houses and small temples around Kannur; it combines dance, song, costume, possession and local myth to honour gods, ancestors and heroes. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/artforms/theyyam-ritual/1/?utm_source=openai))

Performers follow strict vrutham (preparatory rites), wear towering headgears and painted faces (kolam), and enact hundreds of named forms — from gentle Bhagavathi goddesses to violent or fire-bearing theyyams — that are both theatrical and sacred. ([theyyam.entekannur.in](https://theyyam.entekannur.in/?utm_source=openai))

For visitors, Theyyam is an entry into a deeply local world: events are communal, devotional and seasonal (the main season runs across the northern winter months), and respectful observation is essential. Parassinikkadavu’s Sree Muthappan shrine near Kannur is notable for offering dependable daily performances of the Muthappan theyyam. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/theyyamcalendar/?utm_source=openai))
highlights: Hundreds of distinct theyyam forms — from Bhadrakali and Raktha Chamundi to Pottan and Vishnumoorthi.
Spectacular kolam (face and body paint), towering headgear and ritual props.
Fire theyyams: daring feats with burning embers and pyres performed at select kavus.
Daily Muthappan performances at Parassinikkadavu — the most reliable way for visitors to see a theyyam.
Events are community rituals: expect songs (thottam), drumming and offerings, not a staged theatre.

sections.heading: Background
body: Theyyam (from Malayalam deivam, ‘divine’) grew in the Kolathunadu area and remains strongest in Kannur and neighbouring Kasaragod; it mixes local myths, caste- and community-based deities, and folk narratives into ritual theatre. Scholars and tourism guides note its continuity as a living cult rather than a museum piece. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/artforms/theyyam-ritual/1/?utm_source=openai))

Thottam (opening songs), ritual fasting and strict preparations precede the transformation, after which the performer speaks or acts as the deity — giving blessings, settling disputes or receiving offerings — within the community context. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/artforms/theyyam-ritual/1/?utm_source=openai))

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Attend a seasonal theyyam at a kavu to see full rituals, or visit Parassinikkadavu Sree Muthappan Temple for daily morning/evening Muthappan performances when you need a reliable visit option. ([theyyam.entekannur.in](https://theyyam.entekannur.in/kavu/parassinikkadavu-sree-muthappan-temple?utm_source=openai))

Look and listen for the sequence: thottam (legendary song), costume/kolam, the moment of possession, and any act-specific feats (fire-leaping, bed-of-embers, swordplay). Photographs are often possible, but follow local rules and requests from priests or elders. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/artforms/theyyam-ritual/1/?utm_source=openai))

Plan to visit well-known kavus in and around Kannur (Muchilottu, Kalarivathukkal, Kottiyoor area events, and many small local kavus) — local theyyam calendars list dates and locations each season. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/theyyamcalendar/?utm_source=openai))

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Best time: the theyyam season runs roughly from October/November to March/May depending on local calendars; peak activity and big festivals usually fall in the northern winter months — check that season’s calendar before you travel. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/theyyamcalendar/?utm_source=openai))

How to reach kavus around Kannur: fly to Kannur International Airport (Mattannur), use Kannur railway station, or take road connections from Kannur town; local buses and taxis connect to most kavus and shrines. For dependable performances, Parassinikkadavu is about 18 km from Kannur town. Confirm local transport and timings in advance. ([travelkannur.in](https://travelkannur.in/theyyam.html?utm_source=openai))

Respect local customs: arrive early (rituals follow a strict order), remove footwear at the kavu, avoid loud behaviour near the deity, ask before photographing, and follow any instructions from temple authorities or elders. ([hellokerala.online](https://hellokerala.online/stories/theyyam-a-guide?utm_source=openai))

latest.text: Kerala Tourism and local theyyam calendars for the 2026–27 season are published online — check the calendar for temple dates and confirmed kavu programs before you travel.
Kannur guides note Parassinikkadavu Sree Muthappan Temple continues to offer daily Muthappan theyyam performances (morning & evening), making it the most reliable visitor option.
Kerala’s Department of Museums & Zoos lists a Theyyam Museum at Kannur as an ongoing project (construction/works reported in recent departmental updates).

visitorInfo.bestTime: Main theyyam season: roughly October/November through March/May; peak festival activity in the northern winter months.
visitorInfo.howToReach: Fly to Kannur International Airport (Mattannur) or arrive by train at Kannur station; local buses, taxis and hired vehicles reach major kavus. For reliable viewing, Parassinikkadavu is ~18 km from Kannur town. ([travelkannur.in](https://travelkannur.in/theyyam.html?utm_source=openai))
etiquette: Approach as a guest: theyyam is a living community ritual — behave respectfully, remove shoes, and follow instructions from elders or priests. ([hellokerala.online](https://hellokerala.online/stories/theyyam-a-guide?utm_source=openai))

Ask before photographing — some moments and shrines restrict cameras or ask for permission; avoid flash near performers. ([hellokerala.online](https://hellokerala.online/stories/theyyam-a-guide?utm_source=openai))

Check a local theyyam calendar (Kerala Tourism / local kavu listings) for exact dates; small kavus may change schedules, so confirm before you travel. ([keralatourism.org](https://www.keralatourism.org/theyyamcalendar/?utm_source=openai))

If you want a dependable show, plan for Parassinikkadavu’s Muthappan performances (daily) rather than relying on small rural kavus unless you have local contacts. ([theyyam.entekannur.in](https://theyyam.entekannur.in/kavu/parassinikkadavu-sree-muthappan-temple?utm_source=openai))
